H., Firat, O., Auli, M., Ruder, S., Riesa, J., Johnson, M. (2022). XTREME-S: Evaluating Cross-lingual Speech Representations. arXiv.
creator: Alexis Conneau, Ankur Bapna, Yu Zhang, Min Ma, Patrick von Platen, Anton Lozhkov, Colin Cherry, Ye Jia, Clara Rivera, Mihir Kale, Daan Van Esch, Vera Axelrod, Simran Khanuja, Jonathan H. Clark, Orhan Firat, Michael Auli, Sebastian Ruder, Jason Riesa, Melvin Johnson (Google Research, Hugging Face, Meta AI)
description: XTREME-S is a benchmark for evaluating cross-lingual speech representations. It covers four task families—speech recognition, classification, speech-to-text translation and retrieval—across 102 languages, 3 domains, and includes the new Fleurs evaluation dataset.
name: XTREME-S
rai:annotationsPerItem: For Fleurs, the benchmark uses 2009 parallel sentences and collects between one and three recordings for each sentence (2.3 on average).
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: For the new Fleurs component, the authors use 2009 n-way parallel sentences from the FLoRes dev and devtest sets in 102 languages, collect between one and three recordings per sentence, build train/dev/test splits with 1509/150/350 sentences, and ensure speakers in train are different from speakers in dev/test.
rai:dataBiases: The benchmark is designed to reduce bias toward high-resource settings by covering 102 diverse languages, more than 10 language families, multiple domains, and low-resource conditions. The authors note stronger results for Western European languages than for Sub-Saharan African or South Asian groups, highlighting imbalance due in part to larger amounts of unlabeled data in Western European languages.
rai:dataCollection: XTREME-S is assembled by grouping publicly available multilingual speech datasets across four task families: Fleurs, MLS, VoxPopuli, CoVoST-2, and Minds-14. For Fleurs, the authors additionally collect speech recordings for 2009 parallel FLoRes sentences in 102 languages and define new train/dev/test splits.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: The benchmark draws on raw/source speech and text from existing datasets and corpora, including read speech, parliamentary speech, e-banking spoken data, and FLoRes dev/devtest sentences. For Fleurs retrieval, transcription candidates are augmented with 100k sentences from Wikipedia, and the paper also mentions CommonCrawl in the retrieval pool description.
rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis, Manual Human Curator
rai:dataLimitations: The benchmark focuses on linguistic aspects of speech and does not evaluate nonlinguistic/paralinguistic aspects such as speech synthesis or voice conversion. The authors also note remaining performance gaps across geographical language groups and caution against overfitting on open test sets.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: The benchmark merges monolingual Minds-14 datasets into a single multilingual dataset with a 30-20-50% train-dev-test split. For Fleurs, the authors create new train/dev/test splits; for retrieval, they augment candidate pools with 100k Wikipedia sentences and describe fine-tuning with a ranking loss.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: When needed, the authors provide scripts to download data and reproduce preprocessing steps. The benchmark also uses new train/dev/test splits for Fleurs and merged multilingual splits for Minds-14.
rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The paper states that results on the speech retrieval task will be updated in the next version of the paper, that additional test sets may be added in the future, and that FLEURS may receive a second version with fixes for missing or low-quality recordings, with updates made on their platform.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The authors motivate multilingual speech technology as important for giving speakers of under-represented languages an equal voice on the Internet and enabling their content and culture to be known outside their language cluster. They hope the benchmark will accelerate data-efficient speech technology for all the world’s languages.
rai:dataUseCases: XTREME-S is intended for evaluating multilingual speech representations and cross-lingual transfer across speech recognition, speech translation, speech classification, and speech retrieval tasks.
